newsitem.title: USA: CSCE world sugar ends lower, rally waning.
newsitem.headline: CSCE world sugar ends lower, rally waning.

text.p: CSCE world sugar futures ended lower Monday, after a choppy but high volume session, which cast doubt on how much momentum remains in the six week old rally, traders said.
CSCE May sugar ended down 0.13 cent at 10.84 cents a pound, after seeing an 11.08-10.68 cent range.
The May/July backwardation ended around 0.21 cent down from 0.25 cent Friday.
"It was a very technically-motivated session," one trade house broker said.
"(May sugar) was stopped at its high by heavy producer selling and once it dropped below unchanged it became technically negative," he said.
"The specs have a large long position right now, so they're just getting out."
The net long position held by "large traders" in CSCE sugar rose to 29,960 lots by February 25, a turnaround from a net short position of 8,015 lots two weeks earlier.
But total open interest has fallen during the rally, with the trade seen lifting long hedges as prices rose.
CSCE May sugar saw a high at 11.19 cents on February 20, before a correction to the six week uptrend was seen in late February.
While the market has since returned from an overbought condition, Monday's failure to hold above Friday's highs by the close, cast doubt on how much longer the rally may last, analysts said.
Recent strength has been driven by buying the physical market from Iran in particular, which may have bought as much as 300,000 tonnes in the last three months.
Iraq is also expected to be a buyer under the UN's oil-for-food deal and has set a tender for 120,000 tonnes of white sugar.
China has also been reported buying sugar for re-export.
Adding to the strength was a report that Brazil removed some 500,000 tonnes of sugar from the export quota and put it back into the domestic market.

But longer term though global production is still seen outpacing consumption, while stocks as a percentage of demand are at the highest level since the mid-1980's when prices were trading at much lower levels, analysts said.

"There is little doubt that world sugar stocks will increase in 1996/97, with surplus forecasts released by various statistical sources ranging from two to three million tonnes," Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said.

However much of the anticipated surplus may not actually be available to the market, as Indian stocks account for most of the forecast surplus and the Indian government is seen unlikely to authorize sales from stockpiles.

World sugar production in 1996/97 (October/September) should reach 123.34 million tonnes raw value, little changed from 123.90 million tonnes the previous season, according to International Sugar Organization (ISO) data late last week.
The ISO forecast a sugar surplus of 2.80 million tonnes for 1996/97, though this was sharply lower than the previous year's surplus of 5.94 million tonnes.
((-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, +1-212-859-1640))
